key_terms.meaning: Thin region near a solid surface where velocity rises from zero at the wall to the free-stream value U∞.
At a solid wall the fluid velocity equals the wall velocity; for a fixed wall, u = 0.
Distance from the wall where the velocity u reaches about 0.99U∞.
δ* = ∫₀^∞ (1 − u/U∞) dy; the distance the wall would be shifted to give the same mass-flow deficit.
θ = ∫₀^∞ (u/U∞)(1 − u/U∞) dy; a length measuring the momentum-flow deficit.
δ_E = ∫₀^∞ (u/U∞)(1 − (u/U∞)²) dy; a length measuring the kinetic-energy-flow deficit.
Smooth, orderly layer near the leading edge where viscous shear dominates and Re_x is below the critical value.
Chaotic layer with eddy mixing and a flatter mean velocity profile, occurring above a critical Re_x.
Very thin viscous film next to the wall inside a turbulent boundary layer where the velocity changes rapidly.
Pressure increasing in the flow direction (dp/dx > 0), which slows the near-wall fluid.
Breakaway of the boundary layer from the surface when near-wall fluid reverses under an adverse pressure gradient.
Drag caused by pressure differences around a body, especially the low-pressure wake after separation.
A base quantity such as mass M, length L, time T or temperature Θ from which other dimensions are built.
Every term in a correct physical equation has the same dimensions.
A power-product method that writes one variable as C times products of others raised to unknown exponents and solves them by matching dimensions.
If a problem has n variables and m fundamental dimensions, it reduces to n − m independent dimensionless π groups.
Re = ρUL/μ = UL/ν, the ratio of inertial force to viscous force.
Model and prototype have the same shape with all lengths in a fixed scale ratio.
Model and prototype have similar velocity fields with corresponding velocities in a fixed ratio.
Model and prototype have corresponding force ratios equal, usually achieved by matching the controlling dimensionless group.

takeaways: Viscosity plus the no-slip condition forces a thin boundary layer to grow along a flat plate.
The displacement, momentum and energy thicknesses turn three flow deficits into three lengths.
Laminar flow near the leading edge gives way to turbulence above a critical Reynolds number, but a laminar sublayer remains at the wall.
An adverse pressure gradient can stop and reverse the near-wall flow, causing separation, a wake and extra form drag.
Dimensions are products of powers of M, L, T and Θ, and every correct equation is dimensionally homogeneous.
Rayleigh's method solves exponents for a guessed power product; the Buckingham Pi theorem reduces many variables to n − m π groups.
A dimensionless number is a force or energy ratio, and its size shows which physics controls the flow.
Model testing needs geometric, kinematic and dynamic similarity, usually by matching the one controlling dimensionless group.
bank_note: Long answers usually expect clear definitions, a labelled sketch, the governing dimensionless ratio, and a worked reduction or model-scale calculation; boundary-layer drag and similarity are the common high-mark parts.

bank.q: Define a boundary layer over a flat plate. Explain why it forms and how its thickness grows with distance from the leading edge.
outline: No-slip condition and viscosity
Velocity profile from zero at wall to U∞
δ grows with distance x
Layer stays thin compared with plate length

bank.q: Define displacement thickness, momentum thickness and energy thickness. State the formula and physical meaning of each.
outline: δ* integral and mass-flow deficit
θ integral and momentum-flow deficit
δ_E integral and energy-flow deficit
All three have units of length

bank.q: Describe the laminar and turbulent boundary layers and the laminar sublayer. Mention the role of the critical Reynolds number.
outline: Laminar layer near leading edge
Transition above critical Re_x
Turbulent eddy mixing and flatter profile
Thin viscous sublayer at the wall

bank.q: Explain fundamental dimensions and dimensional homogeneity. Show with two examples why every correct equation must be homogeneous.
outline: Base dimensions M, L, T and Θ
Quantities written as powers of dimensions
Both sides of an equation must match
Examples such as F = ma and pressure = force/area

bank.q: Using Rayleigh's method, derive an expression for the drag force on a flat plate in terms of velocity, length, density and viscosity, leaving the result in dimensionless form.
outline: Assume F = C U^a L^b ρ^c μ^d
Write dimensions of each quantity
Solve exponents by dimensional homogeneity
Obtain F/(ρU²L²) as a function of Re

bank.q: A pipe-flow problem has pressure drop Δp depending on diameter D, length L, velocity V, density ρ and viscosity μ. Use the Buckingham Pi theorem to obtain the dimensionless groups.
outline: n = 6 and m = 3
Choose repeating variables
Form n − m = 3 π groups
Expect Δp/(ρV²), L/D and Re

bank.q: For a linear velocity profile u/U∞ = y/δ in a laminar boundary layer, calculate δ*, θ and the shape factor H. State the assumptions.
outline: Integrate for δ*
Integrate for θ
H = δ*/θ
Linear profile gives δ* = δ/2, θ = δ/6 and H = 3

bank.q: A 1:20 scale model of a ship is tested in water. Explain which similarity law you would match, how you would predict prototype resistance, and why exact similarity may be impossible.
outline: Geometric similarity between model and ship
Froude number matching for free-surface flow
Scale force or resistance to prototype
Reynolds conflict and possible distorted model

bank.q: Explain boundary-layer separation with a sketch of the velocity profiles near the wall. List three methods used to delay separation on a body.
outline: Adverse pressure gradient slows near-wall fluid
Velocity profile reaches zero then reverses
Wake and form drag appear
Streamlining, suction, roughness trip or blowing

bank.q: Analyse how an adverse pressure gradient changes the near-wall velocity profile and leads to form drag. Compare a streamlined body with a bluff body.
outline: dp/dx > 0 slows the fluid near the wall
Separation creates a low-pressure wake
Pressure drag dominates bluff bodies
Streamlined bodies delay separation and reduce form drag

bank.q: Evaluate the statement: 'A model is dynamically similar when all forces are in the same ratio.' Explain why in practice only the controlling dimensionless group is matched.
outline: Dynamic similarity means equal force ratios
Each force ratio is a dimensionless group
All groups cannot usually be matched at once
Choose the dominant group and accept small scale effects

bank.q: Compare Rayleigh's method and the Buckingham Pi theorem. Give their limitations and explain why the Pi theorem is preferred when many variables are involved.
outline: Rayleigh assumes one power product
Exponent solving becomes difficult with many variables
Pi theorem gives n − m groups systematically
Both use dimensional homogeneity

bank.q: A flat plate is tested in a wind tunnel. Discuss how you would decide whether the boundary layer is laminar or turbulent, how you would estimate drag, and how separation would alter the drag.
outline: Compute Re_x along the plate
Use laminar or turbulent boundary-layer relations
Estimate skin-friction drag from shear or drag coefficient
Separation adds pressure drag and a wake

bank.q: For a scale model of a hydraulic structure, explain geometric, kinematic and dynamic similarity. Show how distorted models are used when the controlling similarity cannot be satisfied exactly.
outline: Geometric similarity fixes length scale ratio
Kinematic similarity fixes velocity ratio
Dynamic similarity fixes force ratio
Distorted models use different length scales in different directions to match the controlling law

glossary.def: The thin region near a solid surface where viscous effects make the velocity change from zero at the wall to the free-stream value.
The condition that fluid in contact with a solid surface has the same velocity as the surface.
The uniform velocity U∞ far from the body and outside the boundary layer.
The distance δ from the wall where the velocity reaches about 0.99U∞.
The length δ* by which the wall would be shifted outward to give the same mass-flow deficit as the real boundary layer.
The length θ that represents the loss of momentum flux in the boundary layer.
The length δ_E that represents the loss of kinetic-energy flux in the boundary layer.
The ratio H = δ*/θ, which measures how full or how sluggish the velocity profile is.
A smooth boundary layer in which fluid particles move in orderly layers and viscous shear dominates.
A boundary layer with chaotic eddies, strong mixing and a flatter mean velocity profile.
A very thin viscous layer next to the wall inside a turbulent boundary layer.
A pressure increase in the flow direction that slows the fluid near the wall.
The detachment of the boundary layer from a surface when near-wall fluid reverses under an adverse pressure gradient.
The low-pressure disturbed region downstream of a separated or bluff body.
Drag due to pressure differences around a body, mainly from the wake behind separation.
Drag due to viscous shear stress along the wetted surface.
A base dimension such as mass M, length L, time T or temperature Θ.
The requirement that all terms of a correct physical equation have the same dimensions.
A dimensional method that assumes a power-law product and solves the unknown exponents.
The rule that n variables with m fundamental dimensions form n − m independent dimensionless groups.
A combination of variables with no net dimension, often a ratio of two forces.
The condition that model and prototype have the same shape with all lengths in one fixed ratio.
The condition that velocities at corresponding points in model and prototype are in a fixed ratio.
The condition that forces at corresponding points in model and prototype are in a fixed ratio.
A model in which the length scale is different in different directions.
